Keep this sheet open during the labs. It covers the Week 6 measures and theories from Chapter 9, plus bivariate mapping and travel-time modelling, which the textbook skips (marked \*).

## Development measures

| Measure | What it is | Watch for |
|---|---|---|
| GNI per capita (PPP) | All income generated by a country, divided by population, adjusted for cost of living | An average; hides how income is shared |
| Purchasing power parity (PPP) | Adjusts prices so a dollar buys the same basket of goods everywhere | Comparing unadjusted incomes overstates gaps |
| Gini coefficient | Income inequality from 0 (equal) to 100 (one person has everything) | South Africa and Brazil are among the most unequal |
| Life expectancy at birth | Years a newborn is expected to live | Pulled down by infant deaths (Week 2) |
| Mean years of schooling | Average schooling of adults aged 25+ | Looks backward |
| Expected years of schooling | Schooling a child entering school can expect | Looks forward |
| Human Development Index (HDI) | Combines health, education and income into a score from 0 to 1 | A composite: check its parts |
| Gender Inequality Index | Maternal mortality, adolescent births, women in parliament, secondary education, labour force participation | Shows gaps national averages hide |
| Sustainable Development Goals | 17 UN goals (2015) spanning economic, social and environmental development | Many indicators, uneven data |
| Extreme poverty | Living on under $1.90 a day (2011 PPP) | 42% of the world in 1981; under 11% in 2013 |

## Theories of development

| Theory | Cause of underdevelopment | Policy response |
|---|---|---|
| Dependency / world systems | Exploitation rooted in colonial trade; core, semi-periphery, periphery | Import substitution industrialization (tariffs, quotas, local manufacturing) |
| Modernization (Rostow, 1960) | Societies pass through 5 stages: traditional → preconditions → take-off → drive to maturity → high mass consumption | Aid, technology transfer, large infrastructure |
| Neoliberalism (Washington Consensus) | Too little market freedom | Fiscal discipline, privatization, deregulation, free trade |
| Density, distance, division (World Bank) | Gains from dense cities; lags with distance from them; barriers between countries | Urban planning, connecting infrastructure, open trade and migration |

The chapter favours market-based explanations; the debate remains active.

## Mapping two variables\*

- **Bivariate map:** classify two variables into 3 classes each and cross them into a 3 × 3 grid of 9 colours. The corner that is high on both marks priority areas, such as poor and far from care.
- **Composite index:** rescale each indicator to 0–1 (value − min) ÷ (max − min), flip any where higher is better if needed, then average. State the indicators, weights and direction.

## Modelling travel time\*

1. Start from where people live (homesteads, population points or small areas).
2. Choose the destinations (clinics, hospitals).
3. Model travel along the network: walking speed, roads by type, public transport where likely, and barriers such as rivers.
4. Calibrate against reported travel times if you have them.
5. Classify into zones (under 30 min, 30–60, 60–90, over 90) and count people in each.

## ArcGIS Online quick steps

Sign in at [emory.maps.arcgis.com](https://emory.maps.arcgis.com). Login instructions and free Esri training are on the [Emory GIS resources page](https://gis.ecds.emory.edu/). Esri renames menus from time to time, so if a label differs, look for the nearest match.

| To do this | Go to |
|---|---|
| Make a bivariate map | Select the layer → Styles → choose two numeric fields → Relationship → set classes (3 × 3) and colours |
| Build a composite index | Show table → add a Double field → Calculate, for example `(($feature.a - min_a) / (max_a - min_a) + ($feature.b - min_b) / (max_b - min_b)) / 2` with the minimum and maximum values you found first |
| Draw travel-time zones | Analysis → Tools → Create Drive-Time Areas, with walking or driving time and breaks such as 30, 60 and 90 minutes (uses credits) |
| Measure time from each home to the nearest clinic | Analysis → Tools → Find Nearest, with travel mode set to walking or driving (uses credits) |
| Count people in each zone | Analysis → Tools → Summarize Within (uses credits) |

## Public health case: Tanser et al. 2006

| Measure | Value |
|---|---|
| Homesteads interviewed and positioned | About 23,000 |
| Model inputs | Walking time, likely public transport use, road network, natural barriers; calibrated with reported travel times |
| Accuracy predicting the clinic used | 91% |
| Median travel time to nearest clinic | 81 minutes |
| Homesteads travelling 1 hour or more | 65% |
| Median travel time to the district hospital | 170 minutes |
| Odds of clinic use, within 30 min vs 90–120 min | About 10 times higher (adjusted odds ratio 10) |

## Critical lens

- Dependency theory (textbook) traces underdevelopment to colonial trade that extracted raw materials. Many economies still depend on them: 61% of Sierra Leone's GDP came from agricultural exports.
- Under apartheid, rural homelands received far less investment in roads, water and clinics than white areas. Long travel times to care partly reflect that history.
- Ask who defines "development": indices are designed by international institutions, and Washington Consensus conditions were set by lenders.

## Six questions to ask any development map

1. Average or distribution?
2. Which indicators, weighted how?
3. Income in PPP or exchange rates?
4. Straight-line distance or modelled travel time?
5. Which scale hides the people left behind?
6. Whose definition of development?

## Textbook corrections

- The chapter dates NAFTA to 1989. NAFTA was signed in 1992 and took effect in 1994; the 1989 agreement was the Canada–US Free Trade Agreement.
- It places Britain's Rostow "take-off" in the late 1800s. Rostow dated it to the late 1700s.
